t: Male hypogonadism, infertility, sexual dysfunction and androgen drugs
sub: LH tells primary from secondary hypogonadism, injected testosterone shuts down sperm, and the nitric oxide pathway explains erectile dysfunction, PDE5 inhibitors and the nitrate warning.

pretest.q: A man has low testosterone and a high LH. Which structure is the most likely site of the lesion?
pretest.why: A failing testis cannot make testosterone, so negative feedback is lost and the pituitary raises LH and FSH. This is primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism, as in Klinefelter syndrome or mumps orchitis.

w.The anterior pituitary: A failing pituitary would release too little LH, so testosterone and LH would both be low. A high LH shows the pituitary still works and is being driven.
w.The hypothalamus: Hypothalamic failure, as in Kallmann syndrome, lowers GnRH and therefore LH and FSH. That gives low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins, not a high LH.
w.The vas deferens: A blocked sperm duct causes obstructive azoospermia but leaves the testes working, so testosterone and LH both stay normal.

pretest.q: Why must sildenafil never be given together with a nitrate?
o: Both raise cGMP and cause profound hypotension
Nitrates inhibit PDE5 and block the drug
Nitrates raise cAMP, which cancels the drug
pretest.why: Nitrates release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP, and sildenafil stops PDE5 from breaking cGMP down. Together they relax vascular smooth muscle so strongly that blood pressure can fall dangerously.

w.Nitrates inhibit PDE5 and block the drug: Nitrates do not act on PDE5. They donate nitric oxide, which feeds the same pathway the drug amplifies, and that is the source of the danger.
w.They compete for alpha-1 receptors: Neither drug acts at alpha-1 receptors. That action belongs to tamsulosin and similar drugs, which add hypotension of their own.
w.Nitrates raise cAMP, which cancels the d: Nitrates work through cGMP, not cAMP. A higher level of either cyclic nucleotide would favor an erection, not cancel the drug.

pretest.q: Which pattern follows months of testosterone injections taken for bodybuilding?
o: Low LH and FSH with small testes
High LH and FSH with small testes
Normal LH and FSH with large testes
pretest.why: Injected testosterone raises the blood level, so the pituitary cuts LH and FSH. Testosterone inside the testis and sperm production then fall, and the testes shrink.

w.High LH and FSH with small testes: This is the primary hypogonadism pattern, seen when the testis itself has failed. Outside androgens shut the pituitary down instead of driving it.
w.High LH with normal testes: A high LH would mean the pituitary senses too little testosterone, which is the opposite of what an injected androgen causes.
w.Normal LH and FSH with large testes: Without LH and FSH to drive them, the testes shrink instead of enlarging, so large testes with normal hormones would not follow androgen injections.

body: How do primary and secondary hypogonadism differ?

Hypogonadism means low testosterone, with low libido, fatigue and muscle loss. Testosterone is low in every type, so luteinizing hormone (LH) tells you where the problem is. In {{rp22_primary|primary hypogonadism}} the testis has failed. The pituitary senses the low testosterone and pushes harder, so LH and FSH are high (**hypergonadotropic**). Causes are Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY: tall, small firm testes, gynecomastia), mumps orchitis, chemotherapy, radiation, torsion and cryptorchidism. In {{rp22_secondary|secondary hypogonadism}} the hypothalamus or pituitary has failed, so LH and FSH are low or inappropriately normal (**hypogonadotropic**). Causes are Kallmann syndrome with anosmia, a pituitary tumor, hyperprolactinemia, opioids, glucocorticoids, obesity, hemochromatosis and exogenous androgens. Prolactin excess and opioids both suppress GnRH pulses.

The Sertoli cells of the tubules make {{rp22_inhibin|inhibin B}}, which holds FSH down without changing LH. So when the tubules fail but the Leydig cells still work, FSH rises even though testosterone is normal.
Total testosterone can mislead when SHBG is abnormal

Most testosterone in blood is bound, tightly to {{rp22_shbg|SHBG}} and loosely to albumin, so only 2 to 3% is free and active. SHBG falls in obesity, diabetes and hypothyroidism, which lowers total testosterone while the free level may stay normal. SHBG rises with aging, hyperthyroidism, cirrhosis and estrogens, which hides a low free level behind a normal total. When SHBG is likely to be off, measure free testosterone or calculate it from total testosterone, SHBG and albumin.
What do exogenous androgens and testosterone therapy do?

Injected testosterone, gels and **anabolic steroids** raise the blood level, so the pituitary cuts LH and FSH. The testes shrink and make no sperm (**azoospermia**). Testosterone also raises red cell production, so the hematocrit climbs (polycythemia), and it causes acne, low HDL and mood change. The enzyme aromatase converts some of it to estradiol, which causes gynecomastia. Therapy is for symptomatic men with confirmed low levels, with **monitoring** of hematocrit and PSA. It is avoided in prostate or breast cancer and when fertility is wanted. In that case clomiphene (a SERM that blocks estrogen feedback) or hCG (an LH analog) raises the testis's own output instead.
Why does injected testosterone cause infertility when testosterone drives spermatogenesis?

Sperm production needs a testosterone level inside the seminiferous tubules that is about 50 to 100 times higher than in blood. Leydig cells make it only when LH tells them to. Injected testosterone raises the blood level, so the hypothalamus and pituitary cut GnRH, LH and FSH. Without LH, the Leydig cells go quiet and testosterone inside the testis collapses. Without FSH, the Sertoli cells lose support. The testes shrink and sperm disappear. Recovery takes months and is sometimes incomplete, so hCG or clomiphene is used when fertility matters.
What causes male infertility, and how is azoospermia read?

The first test is a **semen analysis**. Spermatogenesis takes about 74 days, plus 10 to 14 days in the epididymis, so a sample reflects events from about three months earlier. Causes are pretesticular (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia, exogenous androgens), testicular (Klinefelter syndrome, Y microdeletions, cryptorchidism, mumps, toxins) and posttesticular (vasectomy, duct obstruction, retrograde ejaculation). The most common correctable cause is varicocele, a tangle of dilated veins, usually on the left. Immotile sperm with chronic sinusitis suggest Kartagener syndrome.

In azoospermia (no sperm in the ejaculate), testis size and FSH tell the story. **Obstructive** azoospermia has normal testes and normal FSH, because sperm are made but cannot get out. Non-obstructive azoospermia means the Sertoli and germ cells have failed, so the testes are small and soft and FSH is high.

Semen volume gives another clue. The seminal vesicles supply most of the volume and all of the fructose. So a low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative ejaculate with no sperm means their fluid is missing. The cause is ejaculatory duct obstruction or {{rp22_cbavd|congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens}} (CBAVD). CBAVD is usually due to CFTR mutations, so both partners need cystic fibrosis carrier testing. The testes work, so FSH and testis size stay normal. A low-volume ejaculate with sperm in the urine afterward is retrograde ejaculation, caused by alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin, diabetic autonomic neuropathy or prostate surgery.
Working up an infertile man in order
Repeat the semen analysis, then read volume, pH and fructose
Two abnormal samples a month apart confirm the problem. Low volume, acidic pH and no fructose point to duct obstruction or CBAVD.
Examine, then measure testosterone, LH, FSH and prolactin
Check the vas deferens, testis size and any varicocele. Low LH and FSH point to a pretesticular cause, and a high FSH points to testicular failure.
Add genetics if sperm are absent or very few
Order a karyotype for Klinefelter syndrome and testing for Y microdeletions. Test for CFTR mutations when the vas is absent.
A testicular biopsy shows where sperm production stops. The patterns to know are {{rp22_ma|maturation arrest}} and Sertoli cell-only tubules.
Germ cells stop at one stage, usually the primary spermatocyte
Genetic or toxic block of meiosis
Only Sertoli cells, no germ cells
Thick basement membrane, fibrosis, clustered Leydig cells

body.q: A man with azoospermia has semen volume 0.8 mL, acidic pH and no fructose, and normal testis size and FSH. Which reasoning best explains these findings?
o: Testicular failure has shrunk the semen volume, and the pituitary has brought FSH back to normal
Seminal vesicle fluid, the source of fructose and most of the volume, is missing from duct obstruction or an absent vas, while the testes work normally
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism has removed testosterone support, so sperm production stopped but FSH looks normal
A varicocele has raised testicular temperature, which impairs spermatogenesis and lowers the fructose in semen
body.why: The seminal vesicles make most of the ejaculate volume, an alkaline fluid rich in fructose, and the prostate adds a slightly acidic fluid. If the ejaculatory ducts are blocked or the vas and vesicles are absent (CBAVD), the ejaculate is small, acidic and fructose-negative. The testes are untouched, so testis size and FSH stay normal. Testicular failure would raise FSH, and hypogonadotropic disease would lower it.

body: How do erection and ejaculation work, and why does erectile dysfunction matter?

An erection is a parasympathetic reflex through sacral nerves S2 to S4. Nerves and the endothelium release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP and relaxes the smooth muscle of the penis. The sinusoids fill with blood and squeeze the veins against the tunica albuginea, so the blood stays in. Emission is sympathetic (T10 to L2), and ejaculation is somatic through the pudendal nerve. **Erectile dysfunction** is most often vascular (atherosclerosis, diabetes, hypertension, smoking), then neurogenic, hormonal, drug-induced (thiazides, beta-blockers, spironolactone, SSRIs) or psychogenic. Preserved nocturnal and morning erections suggest a psychogenic cause, while gradual loss of them suggests an organic one. Because penile arteries are narrower than coronary arteries, new erectile dysfunction can come before a heart attack.
Back pain, myalgia (PDE11); daily dose also treats BPH
PDE5 inhibitor, fastest onset, most selective
Given in the penis or urethra; pain, fibrosis, priapism

PDE5 inhibitors amplify nitric oxide signaling but do not create it, so they need sexual stimulation. Never combine one with a **nitrate**. Both raise cGMP, so blood pressure can fall dangerously. Wait 24 hours after sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil. Alpha-blockers also add to the hypotension. Rare harms are NAION, an ischemic optic neuropathy that causes sudden vision loss, and sudden hearing loss. If the tunica is scarred, venous leak makes these drugs fail. Alprostadil, which works by a different pathway, is then the next step.
How do alpha-1 blockers and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors work?

Alpha-1 receptors, mostly the alpha-1A subtype, keep the prostate and bladder neck tight. Alpha-1B receptors on vessels keep blood pressure up. **Alpha-1 blockers** relax the first, which eases urine flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and lower the second. Tamsulosin and silodosin are alpha-1A selective, so they spare blood pressure. They do impair emission and bladder neck closure, causing retrograde or absent ejaculation with a normal orgasm, and they cause floppy iris syndrome at cataract surgery. Terazosin and doxazosin are nonselective and also treat hypertension. They cause **orthostatic** hypotension and first-dose syncope, so the first dose is taken at bedtime.

**5-alpha-reductase inhibitors** block the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT. Finasteride inhibits type 2, found in the prostate and genital skin, and dutasteride inhibits types 1 and 2. They shrink an enlarged prostate over months and lower the risk of retention and surgery, but they do not relax the muscle, so they work slowly. They halve PSA, so the measured value is doubled. Adverse effects are lower libido, erectile dysfunction, less ejaculate and gynecomastia. They are teratogenic, because DHT forms the male external genitalia, so pregnant women must not handle crushed tablets. A lower dose of finasteride treats male-pattern baldness.
How do SSRIs and other drugs change ejaculation and breast tissue?

Premature ejaculation is the most common male sexual dysfunction. Serotonin raises the ejaculation threshold, so SSRIs (paroxetine most) and clomipramine help. The same effect is an adverse effect of SSRIs given for depression: delayed ejaculation and lower libido, with erections usually intact. Treat any erectile dysfunction first, because a failing erection can mimic premature ejaculation.

Gynecomastia means breast enlargement from a high estrogen-to-androgen ratio. It is normal in newborns, puberty and old age. It is pathologic in Klinefelter syndrome, cirrhosis (the liver clears less estrogen), hCG-secreting testicular tumors, hyperthyroidism and obesity (fat makes estrogen by aromatase). Drugs that cause it include spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, digoxin, marijuana and antiandrogens.
How do antiandrogens and androgen deprivation therapy work?

{{rp22_adt|Androgen deprivation therapy}} (ADT) treats advanced prostate cancer by removing testosterone's growth signal. Leuprolide and goserelin are GnRH agonists. At first they stimulate the pituitary and cause a **flare** of LH and testosterone for one to two weeks. The flare can worsen bone pain or urinary obstruction, so an antiandrogen such as bicalutamide is started first. With continuous exposure, the gonadotrophs (the pituitary cells that make LH and FSH) become desensitized, and testosterone falls to castrate levels. **Abiraterone** inhibits CYP17A1, so cortisol falls and ACTH drives mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia, edema). Prednisone replaces the cortisol and prevents this.
Blocks the androgen receptor and synthesis
Prostate cancer; flutamide is hepatotoxic; cyproterone is also a progestin
GnRH agonist; continuous dosing desensitizes the pituitary
Inhibits CYP17A1 in the testis, adrenal and tumor

Because ADT removes androgens, it causes the problems of hypogonadism: **hot flashes**, lost libido and erections, gynecomastia, fatigue and anemia. It also causes muscle loss with weight gain, insulin resistance and bone loss.
LH is the fork, so get it before prescribing

A high LH means the testis is the problem, so fertility depends on sperm retrieval. A low or normal LH means the brain or pituitary is the problem, so gonadotropins can often restore sperm, and prolactin and pituitary imaging are checked. Starting testosterone first would hide the LH and shut down sperm production.

grid.q: Which of these fit primary rather than secondary hypogonadism?
items: Feedback on the pituitary is lost
Prolactin excess from a pituitary tumor
